Set disabled prop on ReadOnlyPasswordHashField
Description
	
Currently the django.contrib.auth.forms.UserChangeForm defines a clean_password method that returns the initial password value to prevent (accidental) changes to the password value. It is also documented that custom forms for the User model need to define this method: ​https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.1/topics/auth/customizing/#a-full-example
A while ago the forms.Field base class gained the ​disabled argument to:
[disable] a form field using the disabled HTML attribute so that it won’t be editable by users. Even if a user tampers with the field’s value submitted to the server, it will be ignored in favor of the value from the form’s initial data.
It seems to me that this property could be set to True be default on the ReadOnlyPasswordHashField used to display the password hash. This way the clean_password is no longer necessary and the potential pitfall when using the ReadOnlyPasswordHashField without implementing clean_password is removed.
checker_input.plan:
# Plan

## Goal

Make `django.contrib.auth.forms.ReadOnlyPasswordHashField` disabled by default via `Field.disabled`, so the password hash can no longer be overridden by tampered POST data without a form author needing to duplicate `clean_password()`. Then remove the now-unnecessary `UserChangeForm.clean_password()` and update the docs that tell custom user-model authors to write it.

## Why this works (repository evidence)

- `forms.Field.__init__` accepts `disabled=False` (`django/forms/fields.py:60`, stored at `:87`). When disabled is true:
  - `Field.bound_data` returns the initial value (`django/forms/fields.py:163`).
  - `Field.has_changed` returns `False` (`django/forms/fields.py:179`).
  - `BaseForm._clean_fields` uses `self.get_initial_for_field(field, name)` instead of the submitted widget value (`django/forms/forms.py:381`), so tampered POST data is ignored and `cleaned_data['password']` becomes the initial hash.
- `ReadOnlyPasswordHashField` (`django/contrib/auth/forms.py`) already overrides `bound_data` (returns initial) and `has_changed` (returns `False`). Setting `disabled=True` makes this behavior come from the base class, so `UserChangeForm.clean_password`, which does the same at the form level, becomes redundant.
- The widget is the custom `ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget`, whose template only renders a `<div>` summary (`django/contrib/auth/templates/auth/widgets/read_only_password_hash.html`). `disabled` is emitted through `BoundField.build_widget_attrs` onto that div (`django/forms/boundfield.py:227`); it is harmless on a non-input element.
- In the admin, this field is rendered by `AdminReadonlyField.contents`, which calls `widget.render(field, value)` directly when `widget.read_only` is true (`django/contrib/admin/helpers.py:216`) rather than through `build_widget_attrs`. So the admin user change page keeps rendering the existing summary div unchanged; there is no visual/HTML regression, and the existing assertion in `tests/auth_tests/test_views.py:1268` remains valid.

Verified with the project interpreter: a `ReadOnlyPasswordHashField(disabled=True)` reports `disabled=True`, `required=False`, `bound_data('tampered','initialhash') == 'initialhash'`, `has_changed('a','b') == False`, and a directly rendered form shows the summary div carrying a `disabled` attribute.

## Changes

1. `django/contrib/auth/forms.py` — `ReadOnlyPasswordHashField.__init__`: add a default next to the existing `required` default.

       def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
           kwargs.setdefault("required", False)
           kwargs.setdefault("disabled", True)
           super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)

   Keep the existing `bound_data`/`has_changed` overrides (still correct, and they guard subclasses that pass `disabled=False`). Defaulting is backward compatible: callers can still pass `disabled=False` to opt out.

2. `django/contrib/auth/forms.py` — `UserChangeForm`: remove the `clean_password` method (its comment and `return self.initial.get('password')`), since the disabled field now provides this behavior.

3. `docs/topics/auth/customizing.txt` — in the "A full example" custom user-model block (around lines 1128-1142), remove the `clean_password` method from the example `UserChangeForm`.

4. `docs/releases/3.2.txt` — add a note under the `Forms` section (around line 232) stating that `ReadOnlyPasswordHashField` is now disabled by default and that `UserChangeForm.clean_password()` is no longer required.

## Tests

- `tests/auth_tests/test_forms.py` (`ReadOnlyPasswordHashTest`): add a check that `ReadOnlyPasswordHashField().disabled` is `True` and that `ReadOnlyPasswordHashField(disabled=False)` stays enabled.
- Existing tests should pass unchanged: `UserChangeFormTest.test_bug_19133` (tampered POST ignored, cleaned value is the initial hash) and `test_bug_19349_bound_password_field` (bound field value equals the initial hash). `AdminPasswordChangeFormTest` and other forms are unaffected because `ReadOnlyPasswordHashField` is used only by `UserChangeForm`.
- `tests/auth_tests/test_views.py` admin change-page assertion is unaffected (admin renders the widget directly, see above).
- Run with the frozen environment, e.g. `./tests/runtests.py auth_tests.test_forms`.

## Notes / scope

- Behavior changes only for `ReadOnlyPasswordHashField` instances that do not pass an explicit `disabled`. Custom forms that copy the documented `clean_password` still work (returning the initial value is consistent with a disabled field).
- The redundant `bound_data`/`has_changed` overrides are intentionally left in place; removing them is optional cleanup and not required for the fix.

checker_input.issue_description:
squashmigrations does not unset model options when optimizing CreateModel and AlterModelOptions
Description
	
When an operation resembling AlterModelOptions(name="test_model", options={}) is squashed into the corresponding CreateModel operation, model options are not cleared on the resulting new CreateModel operation object.
CreateModel.reduce() sets the new options as options={**self.options, **operation.options} in this case (django/db/migrations/operations/models.py line 144 on commit 991dce4f), with no logic to remove options not found in operation.options as is found in AlterModelOptions.state_forwards().
I believe this issue still exists on the master branch based on my reading of the code, but I've only tested against 2.2.
checker_input.plan:
# Plan

## Problem

When the migration optimizer folds an `AlterModelOptions` operation into a preceding `CreateModel`, it merges options with a plain dict union:

`django/db/migrations/operations/models.py:139`
```python
elif isinstance(operation, AlterModelOptions) and self.name_lower == operation.name_lower:
    return [
        CreateModel(
            self.name,
            fields=self.fields,
            options={**self.options, **operation.options},
            bases=self.bases,
            managers=self.managers,
        ),
    ]
```

`AlterModelOptions` has emptying semantics defined by its `state_forwards` (`models.py:672`): it updates options with the new values, then removes every key in `AlterModelOptions.ALTER_OPTION_KEYS` that is absent from the operation's `options`. The `reduce` path above has no equivalent removal step, so unsquashing an `AlterModelOptions(name=..., options={})` leaves the removed keys on the resulting `CreateModel`.

Concrete demonstration run against the frozen tree: `CreateModel('Foo', ..., options={'verbose_name': 'Foo', 'ordering': ['id'], 'managed': True})` followed by `AlterModelOptions('Foo', {})` optimizes to a `CreateModel` that still carries all three options. Applying the whole sequence through `state_forwards` yields options `{'indexes': [], 'constraints': []}`, while applying the optimized single operation yields `{'verbose_name': 'Foo', 'ordering': ['id'], 'managed': True, 'indexes': [], 'constraints': []}`. They differ, confirming the bug.

## Fix

In `CreateModel.reduce`, make the `AlterModelOptions` branch mirror `AlterModelOptions.state_forwards` before constructing the new `CreateModel`:

```python
elif isinstance(operation, AlterModelOptions) and self.name_lower == operation.name_lower:
    options = self.options.copy()
    for key in operation.ALTER_OPTION_KEYS:
        if key not in operation.options:
            options.pop(key, False)
    options.update(operation.options)
    return [
        CreateModel(
            self.name,
            fields=self.fields,
            options=options,
            bases=self.bases,
            managers=self.managers,
        ),
    ]
```

Notes on the mechanics, verified by running the patched method:
- Only the model-level keys in `ALTER_OPTION_KEYS` are candidates for removal. Options outside that list (e.g. `unique_together`, `index_together`, `order_with_respect_to`) are preserved, matching `state_forwards`.
- `options.pop(key, False)` is used for consistency with `AlterModelOptions.state_forwards`; a plain `.pop(key, None)` would behave identically here.
- `options.update(operation.options)` must run after the removal loop so an explicitly provided option (even one equal to `{}`) is retained.

With this change, the three representative cases all make the optimized sequence state-equivalent to the original:
- `AlterModelOptions('Foo', {})` clears all `ALTER_OPTION_KEYS` (e.g. `verbose_name`, `ordering`, `managed`).
- Partial override (`{'ordering': ['name']}`) keeps other keys and applies the new value.
- Non-destructive override (`{'verbose_name_plural': 'Foozes'}`) preserves `verbose_name`, so the existing `test_create_alter_model_options` expectation is unchanged.

`CreateModel.deconstruct()` omits `options` when falsy, so an emptied result serializes without an `options` kwarg — the desired behavior.

## Tests

Add a regression case to `tests/migrations/test_optimizer.py`, next to the existing `test_create_alter_model_options` (around line 111), covering the emptying behavior. Model it on that test's anonymous `CreateModel`/`AlterModelOptions` construction and `assertOptimizesTo`, e.g. a `CreateModel('Foo', fields=[], options={'verbose_name': 'Foo', 'ordering': ['id']})` followed by `AlterModelOptions('Foo', {})` should optimize to `CreateModel('Foo', fields=[])` with no options.

The fix is localized to `CreateModel.reduce`; no changes are needed in `AlterModelOptions`, the autodetector, or `AlterTogetherOptionOperation`/`AlterOrderWithRespectTo` branches (those options are not part of `ALTER_OPTION_KEYS`).

## Verification

- Run `tests/migrations/test_optimizer.py` and `tests/migrations/test_operations.py` with `/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python`.
- A useful sanity check (already used to confirm the root cause and the proposed patch): apply the original operation list and the optimized result through `ProjectState.state_forwards` and assert the resulting model `.options` are equal.

checker_input.issue_description:
add filter is unable to concatenate strings with lazy string
Description
	
If you try to concatenate a string with a lazy string with the add template filter, the result is always the empty string because the add filter generates an exception (TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "__proxy__") to str).
checker_input.plan:
# Plan

## Problem

`{{ "foo"|add:lazy_string }}` always renders as `""`. The `add` filter falls back to `value + arg` when both arguments can't be coerced to `int`, and Python's `str.__add__` refuses to concatenate with a lazy proxy object:

```
>>> from django.utils.functional import lazystr
>>> lazystr('bar') + 'foo'   # works, __add__ is proxied
'barfoo'
>>> 'foo' + lazystr('bar')   # TypeError: must be str, not __proxy__
```

`add()` swallows the exception and returns `''`:

```python
# django/template/defaultfilters.py, line 675
@register.filter(is_safe=False)
def add(value, arg):
    """Add the arg to the value."""
    try:
        return int(value) + int(arg)
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        try:
            return value + arg
        except Exception:
            return ''
```

## Root cause

`lazy()` builds a per-callable `__proxy__` class in `django/utils/functional.py`. `__prepare_class__` clones every attribute of the proxied class's MRO onto the proxy—including `str.__add__`—but nothing provides `__radd__`. So `lazy_str + str` works, while `str + lazy_str` (which needs the reflected operand hook on the proxy) raises `TypeError`. The filter then silently turns that into `''`.

## Proposed change

Add explicit `__add__` and `__radd__` methods to the `__proxy__` class in `django/utils/functional.py`, immediately after the existing `__mod__` method (around line 174) and before `__deepcopy__` (line 179):

```python
        def __add__(self, other):
            if self._delegate_text:
                return str(self) + other
            return self.__cast() + other

        def __radd__(self, other):
            if self._delegate_text:
                return other + str(self)
            return other + self.__cast()
```

Why this location and shape:

- Defining `__add__`/`__radd__` directly in the class body mirrors the existing hand-written `__str__`, `__eq__`, `__mod__` overrides. `__prepare_class__` skips any attribute already present on the class (`if hasattr(cls, method_name): continue`), so these definitions take precedence over the auto-generated `str.__add__` promise.
- The `self._delegate_text` branch keeps behavior consistent with `__mod__` / `__str__` for text-returning lazy objects, while non-text lazy objects (e.g. `lazy(..., list)`) are allowed to add against their evaluated value.

I verified locally (patching the file, running under `/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python`, then reverting) that with these two methods:

- `'foo' + lazystr('bar')` → `'foobar'`
- `lazystr('bar') + 'foo'` → `'barfoo'`
- `add('foo', lazystr('bar'))` → `'foobar'`
- `add(lazystr('bar'), 'foo')` → `'barfoo'`
- `[0] + lazy(lambda: [1, 2], list)()` → `[0, 1, 2]`
- integer path `add(1, lazystr('bar'))` still returns `''`, unchanged

Existing suites `template_tests.filter_tests.test_add` and `utils_tests.test_functional` pass unchanged.

## Tests to add

1. In `tests/template_tests/filter_tests/test_add.py`, following the existing `@setup(...)` pattern: a case rendering `{{ s|add:lazy }}` where `lazy` is a `lazystr`, asserting the concatenated string is produced (e.g. `'foo'|add:lazystr('bar')` → `'foobar'`). Import `lazystr` from `django.utils.functional`.
2. In `tests/utils_tests/test_functional.py`, cover the underlying behavior directly: `str + lazy` and `lazy + str` both return the concatenation, and a non-text lazy list concatenates via `+`.

## Release note

Add a short bullet under the "Bugfixes" section of `docs/releases/3.2.txt` describing that lazy strings can now be concatenated with `str`, which fixes the `add` filter silently returning `''`.

## Verification

Run `tests/runtests.py template_tests.filter_tests.test_add utils_tests.test_functional` (pytest is not installed in the provided environment; Django's own runner is available and already used for this repo).

checker_input.plan:
# Plan

## Problem

`DatabaseWrapper.check_constraints()` in `django/db/backends/sqlite3/base.py` builds SQLite `PRAGMA` statements (and a follow-up `SELECT`) by string-formatting raw table/column names **without quoting them**:

```python
violations = chain.from_iterable(
    cursor.execute('PRAGMA foreign_key_check(%s)' % table_name).fetchall()
    for table_name in table_names
)
...
foreign_key = cursor.execute(
    'PRAGMA foreign_key_list(%s)' % table_name
).fetchall()[foreign_key_index]
...
primary_key_value, bad_value = cursor.execute(
    'SELECT %s, %s FROM %s WHERE rowid = %%s' % (
        primary_key_column_name, column_name, table_name
    ),
    (rowid,),
).fetchone()
```

When a table name (or column name) is a SQL keyword such as `order`, SQLite fails to parse the statement: `sqlite3.OperationalError: near "order": syntax error`.

This path is reached during `loaddata`, which calls `connection.check_constraints(table_names=table_names)` (`django/core/management/commands/loaddata.py:131`). That is why loading fixtures for a model named `Order` crashes.

I verified against the bundled SQLite (3.45.3) that:
- `PRAGMA foreign_key_check(order)` → `near "order": syntax error`
- `PRAGMA foreign_key_check("order")` → works (returns violation rows)
- `PRAGMA foreign_key_list(order)` → `near "order": syntax error`
- `PRAGMA foreign_key_list("order")` → works
- Binding a parameter (`PRAGMA foreign_key_check(?)`) does **not** work — PRAGMAs don't accept bound arguments, so quoting/interpolation is the only viable fix.

## Proposed change

Edit `DatabaseWrapper.check_constraints` in `django/db/backends/sqlite3/base.py` to quote identifiers via `self.ops.quote_name(...)`, which the SQLite backend implements as `'"%s"' % name` (idempotent — it returns the name unchanged if already double-quoted; `django/db/backends/sqlite3/operations.py:170`). Quote every interpolated identifier:

- `'PRAGMA foreign_key_check(%s)' % self.ops.quote_name(table_name)`
- `'PRAGMA foreign_key_list(%s)' % self.ops.quote_name(table_name)`
- `'SELECT %s, %s FROM %s WHERE rowid = %%s' % (self.ops.quote_name(primary_key_column_name), self.ops.quote_name(column_name), self.ops.quote_name(table_name))`

This keeps the `%%s` rowid placeholder intact (still bound as a parameter) while making the static identifiers keyword-safe. Quoting the table name fixes the reported bug; quoting the column names (`primary_key_column_name`, `column_name`) and the `FROM` table covers keyword-named columns as well, which is the same class of defect and needed for the query to be correct.

No change is required in `loaddata.py`, the base backend, or the `table_names is None` branch (that branch issues a bare `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` with no table argument).

## Regression test

Add a SQLite-specific test to `tests/backends/sqlite/tests.py` (the `SchemaTests(TransactionTestCase)` class already sets `available_apps = ['backends']`; `isolate_apps` is already imported).

The test should:
1. Define a throwaway model with a keyword table name, e.g. via `@isolate_apps('backends')` and `class Meta: db_table = 'order'`, with a self- or sibling-referencing `ForeignKey`.
2. Create it with the schema editor (`connection.schema_editor()`).
3. With `connection.constraint_checks_disabled()`, insert a row whose FK value has no matching referenced row.
4. Call `connection.check_constraints(table_names=[...])` (the table-name branch, matching the `loaddata` code path) and assert it raises `IntegrityError` rather than `OperationalError`.

Asserting `IntegrityError` (not merely "no `OperationalError`") confirms the quoting fix both parses correctly and still detects the bad reference. A simpler variant that only calls `check_constraints(table_names=['order'])` on a keyword-named table with valid data also reproduces the original `OperationalError`; including one invalid row makes the test meaningful.

Follow existing conventions in this file for schema creation/teardown (see `test_autoincrement` and `test_field_rename_inside_atomic_block`), and guard with the `supports_pragma_foreign_key_check` feature since the `PRAGMA` branch is version-gated (`django/db/backends/sqlite3/features.py:38`).

## Verification

- Run the new test and confirm it fails before the fix with `OperationalError` and passes after.
- Run `tests/backends/tests.py::FkConstraintsTests::test_check_constraints` to confirm no regression in the normal (non-keyword) case.
- Optionally run the broader `tests/backends/` suite.

checker_input.issue_description:
Add --skip-checks option to the runserver command.
Description
	
Rationale:
It would be consistent with other management commands performing system checks
It would help people like me who would rather have checks enabled exclusively in CI/CD than wait 15-20 seconds for each project reload during development
Related StackOverflow question:
​https://stackoverflow.com/questions/41438593/skip-system-checks-on-django-server-in-debug-mode-in-pycharm/41725866
checker_input.plan:
# Plan

## Goal
Add a `--skip-checks` option to the `runserver` management command so developers can start/reload the dev server without paying the per-reload system-check cost.

## Why runserver cannot rely on the framework default
`BaseCommand` only auto-adds the `--skip-checks` argument when `requires_system_checks` is a non-empty sequence (`django/core/management/base.py`, around line 317):

    if self.requires_system_checks:
        parser.add_argument(
            '--skip-checks', action='store_true',
            help='Skip system checks.',
        )

`runserver.Command` deliberately sets `requires_system_checks = []` (its comment: "Validation is called explicitly each time the server is reloaded."), so the framework will **not** add the option for it. `runserver` also does not go through `BaseCommand.execute()`'s check path; it calls the checks itself inside `inner_run`. The `migrate` command is the existing precedent for exactly this situation: it sets `requires_system_checks = []` and manually declares the argument (`django/core/management/commands/migrate.py`):

    parser.add_argument(
        '--skip-checks', action='store_true',
        help='Skip system checks.',
    )

and later gates its own check with `if not options['skip_checks']:`.

## Changes

### 1. `django/core/management/commands/runserver.py`
Add the explicit argument in `Command.add_arguments`, alongside the existing `--noreload`, `--nothreading`, `--ipv6` options:

    parser.add_argument(
        '--skip-checks', action='store_true',
        help='Skip system checks.',
    )

In `inner_run`, gate the explicit checks. The current unconditional block is:

    self.stdout.write("Performing system checks...\n\n")
    self.check(display_num_errors=True)
    # Need to check migrations here, so can't use the
    # requires_migrations_check attribute.
    self.check_migrations()

Change it to run only when not skipped (the "Performing system checks..." banner and `check_migrations()` are part of the same reload cost, so both are skipped):

    if not options['skip_checks']:
        self.stdout.write("Performing system checks...\n\n")
        self.check(display_num_errors=True)
        self.check_migrations()

`options['skip_checks']` is always present because the argument is now declared on this command, and `django/core/management/__init__.py` also injects a default when a command is invoked programmatically via `call_command`.

### 2. `django/contrib/staticfiles/management/commands/runserver.py`
No change required. Its `add_arguments` calls `super().add_arguments(parser)` first, so the new option is inherited automatically. Confirm after the change that `runserver --skip-checks` still starts correctly with staticfiles enabled.

### 3. Tests - `tests/admin_scripts/tests.py`
- The existing `ManageTestserver.test_params_to_runserver` and `test_testserver_handle_params` assert `skip_checks=True` in the `handle()` kwargs; they should continue to pass unchanged because they exercise `testserver` and rely on parser defaults.
- Add a focused test in `ManageRunserver` (the class that already monkeypatches `self.cmd.run`) asserting that with `skip_checks=True` the `inner_run` output does **not** contain "Performing system checks..." and that `check`/`check_migrations` are not called (patch them), and that without the option they are called. This is the behavior the issue is about, so it should be covered.

### 4. Documentation
- `docs/ref/django-admin.txt`: the `runserver` section (around lines 916-1046) documents `--noreload`, `--nothreading`, `--ipv6`. Add a matching `.. django-admin-option:: --skip-checks` entry there describing that it disables the system checks (and migration check) normally run on startup and after each reload.
  - The generic `--skip-checks` text near line 1839 says the option is "only available if the `requires_system_checks` ... attribute is not an empty list or tuple." That statement becomes inaccurate for `runserver`; either soften that generic wording or add a note, so the docs are not self-contradictory.
- `docs/releases/4.0.txt`: under the `Management Commands` heading (line 153), add a bullet noting the new `--skip-checks` option on `runserver`. The repo base commit reports `VERSION = (4, 0, 0, 'alpha', 0)`.

## Verification
- Run the targeted tests: `tests/admin_scripts/tests.py` (the `ManageRunserver`, `ManageTestserver`, and empty-`ALLOWED_HOSTS` cases) using the provided environment at `/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python`, e.g. `/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python tests/runtests.py admin_scripts`.
- Manually confirm `django-admin runserver --skip-checks --noreload` starts without printing the "Performing system checks..." block.

## Open decision for the reviewer
Whether `check_migrations()` should also be suppressed by `--skip-checks`. This plan suppresses it together with the system checks, since it is part of the same per-reload cost and currently runs unconditionally in the same block. If migration warnings should be preserved even when checks are skipped, move `self.check_migrations()` outside the `if not options['skip_checks']:` guard instead.

# Plan

## Bug summary

`BaseHandler.load_middleware()` mutates the local `handler` variable *before* it knows whether the middleware was actually created. If a middleware factory raises `MiddlewareNotUsed`, the `continue` skips the rest of the loop body but already overwrote `handler` with the adapted callable, while `handler_is_async` (which describes that callable) is left at its previous value. The next loop iteration then adapts an already-adapted handler using stale mode information, corrupting the remainder of the middleware chain. In an ASGI/async request this surfaces as a synchronous `HttpResponse` returned where a coroutine is expected — e.g. `TypeError: object HttpResponse can't be used in 'await' expression`, or as the `RuntimeError: You cannot use AsyncToSync in the same thread as an async event loop` observed when reproducing.

The offending code is `django/core/handlers/base.py`, lines 52–65:

```python
            try:
                # Adapt handler, if needed.
                handler = self.adapt_method_mode(
                    middleware_is_async, handler, handler_is_async,
                    debug=settings.DEBUG, name='middleware %s' % middleware_path,
                )
                mw_instance = middleware(handler)
            except MiddlewareNotUsed as exc:
                ...
                continue
```

Only the `handler` assignment is premature; `handler_is_async` is already updated only on success at line 89.

## Proposed change

In `django/core/handlers/base.py`, adapt into a temporary variable and commit it to `handler` only when `middleware()` succeeds, using an `else` clause on the `try`:

```python
            try:
                # Adapt handler, if needed.
                adapted_handler = self.adapt_method_mode(
                    middleware_is_async, handler, handler_is_async,
                    debug=settings.DEBUG, name='middleware %s' % middleware_path,
                )
                mw_instance = middleware(adapted_handler)
            except MiddlewareNotUsed as exc:
                if settings.DEBUG:
                    if str(exc):
                        logger.debug('MiddlewareNotUsed(%r): %s', middleware_path, exc)
                    else:
                        logger.debug('MiddlewareNotUsed: %r', middleware_path)
                continue
            else:
                handler = adapted_handler
```

Everything else in `load_middleware()` (the `process_view` / `process_template_response` / `process_exception` registration and `handler_is_async = middleware_is_async`) already runs only on the success path and needs no change. This makes a skipped middleware a true no-op on the chain state.

## Why this is the right layer

`adapt_method_mode()` is a pure transform: it returns either the original callable or a wrapper and has no side effects, so deferring the assignment is safe. The wrapper created inside the `try` is discarded when `MiddlewareNotUsed` is raised, which is exactly the intent — the skipped middleware should not appear in the chain at all.

No documentation change is warranted. `docs/topics/http/middleware.txt` already documents `sync_capable` / `async_capable` correctly, and a sync-only middleware is meant to work under ASGI (Django adapts it). The defect is purely in the chain bookkeeping.

## Verifying tests

Add a regression test to `tests/middleware_exceptions/tests.py` in the existing `MiddlewareSyncAsyncTests` class. It needs an async request path where one middleware raises `MiddlewareNotUsed`. The repo already has suitable fixtures: `middleware_exceptions.tests.MyMiddleware` raises `MiddlewareNotUsed` in `__init__`, and `middleware_exceptions.middleware.PaymentMiddleware` (sync-only, default flags) sets the status to 402. The scenario to cover:

```python
    @override_settings(MIDDLEWARE=[
        'middleware_exceptions.middleware.PaymentMiddleware',
        'middleware_exceptions.tests.MyMiddleware',
    ])
    async def test_middleware_not_used_async(self):
        response = await self.async_client.get('/middleware_exceptions/view/')
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 402)
```

Notes on reproducing without the fix (verified in this environment):
- With `MIDDLEWARE=['...tests.MyMiddleware', '...middleware.async_payment_middleware']` and an `async_client` request, the pre-fix code raises `RuntimeError: You cannot use AsyncToSync in the same thread as an async event loop`.
- With `MIDDLEWARE=['...middleware.async_payment_middleware', '...tests.MyMiddleware']`, the pre-fix code fails to honor the request, and the post-fix code returns 402.

Choose the ordering that yields the clearest failure before the fix; both exercise the same defect. `PaymentMiddleware` + `MyMiddleware` is closest to the original report (a sync-only middleware skipped inside an async chain).

## How to run

```bash
/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python tests/runtests.py middleware_exceptions --parallel=1
```

Baseline observed on the unmodified tree: 32 tests pass. Expect all existing tests plus the new regression test to pass after the fix; the new test fails before the fix. The environment runs Python 3.6 with an asgiref that supports `async_client`, which the async regression test requires.

## Files touched

- `django/core/handlers/base.py` — defer the `handler` assignment out of the `try`.
- `tests/middleware_exceptions/tests.py` — add the async regression test.

Description
	
Summary
This feature request, for which I will post a PR shortly, aims to improve the specificity of the migration loader's check for and rejection of ​PEP-420 namespace packages. I am NOT asking to allow namespace packages for apps' migrations. I merely want to make the existing check more compliant with Python's documented import API. This would remove one impediment to using Django in so-called frozen Python environments (such as those mentioned in #30950) that do not set ​__file__ on regular packages by default.
This narrow proposal does not change Django's behavior at all for normal Python environments. The only change for frozen environments is that Django will learn how to find existing migrations. In particular, at this time I am not proposing to enable any other Django feature that does not already work in frozen environments.
I would love for this feature to land in Django 3.2.
Details
I initially broached this idea on the ​django-developers mailing list. This is my second ticket related to frozen Python environments, the first being #32177.
The ​current implementation of the migration loader's no-namespace-package check in django.db.migrations.loader.MigrationLoader.load_disk skips searching for migrations in a module m if getattr(m, '__file__', None) is false.
The trouble with this implementation is that namespace packages are not the only modules with no __file__. Indeed, the Python ​documentation states that
__file__ is optional. If set, this attribute's value must be a string. The import system may opt to leave __file__ unset if it has no semantic meaning (e.g. a module loaded from a database).
However, Python's ​documentation also states
Namespace packages do not use an ordinary list for their __path__ attribute. They instead use a custom iterable type....
The class of namespace packages' __path__ in CPython is ​_NamespacePath, but that is a CPython implementation detail. Instead, I propose to augment getattr(m, '__file__', None) with and isinstance(m.__path__, list).

# Plan

## Goal

Change `MigrationLoader.load_disk()` so it rejects only true PEP 420 namespace packages, while still loading migrations from ordinary packages that lack `__file__` (as in frozen Python environments). Do not start loading migrations from namespace packages — the existing namespace behavior must stay unchanged.

## Where the change goes

`django/db/migrations/loader.py`, inside `MigrationLoader.load_disk()`, in the `else:` block that follows the `import_module(module_name)` call (currently lines ~91–99):

```python
            else:
                # Empty directories are namespaces.
                # getattr() needed on PY36 and older (replace w/attribute access).
                if getattr(module, '__file__', None) is None:
                    self.unmigrated_apps.add(app_config.label)
                    continue
                # Module is not a package (e.g. migrations.py).
                if not hasattr(module, '__path__'):
                    self.unmigrated_apps.add(app_config.label)
                    continue
                # Force a reload if it's already loaded (tests need this)
                if was_loaded:
                    reload(module)
```

## Why this is the right discriminator (repository evidence)

I imported the relevant modules in the project environment and observed:

- Regular package (e.g. `migrations.migrations_test_apps.migrated_app.migrations`): `__path__` is a `list`; `isinstance(module.__path__, list)` is `True`.
- Namespace package (e.g. `migrations.test_migrations_namespace_package`, `migrations.faulty_migrations.namespace`, both directories without `__init__.py`): `__file__` is absent and `__path__` is `_frozen_importlib_external._NamespacePath`; `isinstance(module.__path__, list)` is `False`.

Namespaces are therefore distinguishable by `__path__` not being a `list`, not by the absence of `__file__`. The current code conflates the two by keying solely on `__file__`.

## Proposed implementation

Reorder the two guards so `__path__` is known to exist before it is inspected, and make the namespace guard depend on `__path__` not being a `list`:

```python
            else:
                # Module is not a package (e.g. migrations.py).
                if not hasattr(module, '__path__'):
                    self.unmigrated_apps.add(app_config.label)
                    continue
                # Empty directories are namespaces.
                # getattr() needed on PY36 and older (replace w/attribute access).
                if getattr(module, '__file__', None) is None and not isinstance(module.__path__, list):
                    self.unmigrated_apps.add(app_config.label)
                    continue
                # Force a reload if it's already loaded (tests need this)
                if was_loaded:
                    reload(module)
```

Rationale for the reorder: the old `__file__` check ran before the `hasattr(module, '__path__')` check, so it must not be the place where `module.__path__` is dereferenced for non-package modules such as `migrations.py`. Running the "not a package" guard first makes `module.__path__` safe to access in the following guard.

Behavior check against the existing fixtures:

- Namespace package: `__file__` missing and `__path__` is not a `list` → still added to `unmigrated_apps`.
- Regular package without `__file__` (simulated by deleting the attribute): `__file__` missing but `__path__` is a `list` → not skipped, migrations are loaded.
- Normal regular package: `__file__` present → not skipped.
- `migrations.py` module file (`tests/migrations/faulty_migrations/file.py`): no `__path__` → skipped by the reordered guard.

Note on the issue wording: the ticket phrases the extra test as `isinstance(m.__path__, list)`, but that literal positive form would *allow* namespace packages and *reject* regular packages missing `__file__`, contradicting the ticket title and the existing `test_loading_namespace_package` expectation that namespace migrations stay ignored. The negated form (`not isinstance(...)`) is the one consistent with the stated intent, and is what the change above uses.

## Tests

Add a regression test to `LoaderTests` in `tests/migrations/test_loader.py`, next to `test_loading_namespace_package` (~line 505). `unittest.mock` is not currently imported in that file, so add `from unittest import mock` to its imports.

The test should exercise the frozen-package case by clearing `__file__` on an ordinary migrations package and asserting its migrations are still discovered, e.g.:

```python
    @override_settings(MIGRATION_MODULES={'migrations': 'migrations.test_migrations'})
    def test_loading_regular_package_without_file(self):
        """Regular packages without __file__ still load migrations."""
        module = import_module('migrations.test_migrations')
        with mock.patch.object(module, '__file__', None):
            loader = MigrationLoader(connection)
            loader.load_disk()
            migrations = [name for app, name in loader.disk_migrations if app == 'migrations']
            self.assertIn('0001_initial', migrations)
```

Verified in the environment: `import_module('migrations.test_migrations')` returns a cached module whose `__path__` is a `list`, and `mock.patch.object(module, '__file__', None)` makes `getattr(module, '__file__', None)` return `None` while leaving `__path__` a `list`. `import_module` inside `load_disk()` resolves to the same patched cached object; `mock.patch.object` restores `__file__` on exit.

Keep the existing `test_loading_namespace_package` (asserts `migrations == []`), `test_load_empty_dir`, and `test_load_module_file` unchanged; they cover the cases that must not regress.

## Optional documentation

This is a bug fix, so a release note is not required. If one is desired, add a bullet under the `Migrations` section of `docs/releases/3.2.txt` (currently ~line 339) noting that regular packages without `__file__` are no longer treated as namespace packages.

## Verification

Run the loader tests in the project environment from the `tests/` directory:

```
/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python runtests.py migrations.test_loader --verbosity 1
```

Confirm the existing namespace/module-file/empty-dir tests pass along with the new regular-package-without-`__file__` test. These three existing tests already pass on the unmodified tree, so a failure after the change would indicate a regression.

Allow autoreloading of `python -m pkg_other_than_django runserver`
Description
	 
		(last modified by William Schwartz)
	 
​django.utils.autoreload.get_child_arguments detects if Python was launched as python -m django. Currently it detects only when ​-m was passed specifically django (and only in Python environments in which __file__ is set on modules, which is ​not true of all Python environments). Like #32177, this ticket aims to remove one impediment to creating Django-based command-line utilities that have their own ​__main__ sub-module while overriding Django's built-in management commands—in this case, runserver.
The fix, which I have submitted in the ​attached PR, is to use Python's ​documented way of determining if -m was used in get_child_arguments:
The top-level __main__ module is always the entry point of a ​complete Python program.
 __main__.__spec__ is not None ​if and only if Python was launched with -m or the name of a "directory, zipfile or other sys.path entry." In the latter cases, the ​documentation says
If the script name refers to a directory or zipfile, the script name is added to the start of sys.path and the __main__.py file in that location is executed as the __main__ module.
Hence __main__.__spec__.parent (which is ​usually but not always __main__.__package__) exists and is the empty string when Python is started with the name of a directory or zip file.
Therefore Python was started with -m pkg if and only if __main__.__spec__.parent == "pkg".
Following this algorithm is guaranteed to work as long as Python obeys its own documentation, and has the side benefit of avoiding use of __file__.

# Plan

## Goal

Make `django.utils.autoreload.get_child_arguments()` detect *any* `python -m <pkg> ...` invocation (not just `python -m django`), so that a project whose entry point is a custom top-level module (e.g. `python -m myproject runserver`) is correctly restarted by the autoreloader.

## Current implementation and why it fails

`get_child_arguments()` in `django/utils/autoreload.py` (lines 213–247) currently does:

```python
import django.__main__
django_main_path = Path(django.__main__.__file__)
py_script = Path(sys.argv[0])

args = [sys.executable] + ['-W%s' % o for o in sys.warnoptions]
if py_script == django_main_path:
    # The server was started with `python -m django runserver`.
    args += ['-m', 'django']
    args += sys.argv[1:]
elif not py_script.exists():
    ...  # Windows .exe / -script.py fallbacks
else:
    args += sys.argv
return args
```

It only recognizes the `-m django` case, by comparing `sys.argv[0]` against `django.__main__.__file__`. Consequence: `python -m myproject runserver` falls into the final `else` branch and the child process is relaunched as `python myproject/__main__.py ...` (a file path) instead of `python -m myproject ...`, which breaks the reloader for custom top-level packages and also relies on `__file__` (absent in some environments).

## Proposed change

Replace the `django.__main__.__file__` comparison with Python's documented `__main__.__spec__` check. Python sets `__main__.__spec__` when launched with `-m` (or a directory/zip entry point); `__main__.__spec__.parent` is the package name for `-m pkg`, and the empty string for `python <dir>`/`python <zip>`.

Rewrite the branch in `django/utils/autoreload.py` to:

```python
def get_child_arguments():
    """
    Return the executable. This contains a workaround for Windows if the
    executable is reported to not have the .exe extension which can cause bugs
    on reloading.
    """
    import __main__
    py_script = Path(sys.argv[0])

    args = [sys.executable] + ['-W%s' % o for o in sys.warnoptions]
    # __spec__ is set when the server was started with the `-m` option,
    # see https://docs.python.org/3/reference/import.html#main-spec
    # __spec__ may not exist, e.g. when the server is started by a script.
    if __main__.__spec__ is not None and __main__.__spec__.parent:
        args += ['-m', __main__.__spec__.parent]
        args += sys.argv[1:]
    elif not py_script.exists():
        # sys.argv[0] may not exist for several reasons on Windows.
        # ... (existing .exe / -script.py fallback, unchanged)
    else:
        args += sys.argv
    return args
```

Notes on the branch logic:
- `-m django`: `parent == 'django'` → produces `[python, '-m', 'django', *argv[1:]]`, matching today's behavior.
- `-m myproject`: `parent == 'myproject'` → `[python, '-m', 'myproject', *argv[1:]]`. This is the new capability.
- `python <dir>` / `python <zip>`: `parent == ''` (falsy) → falls through to the existing branches; `sys.argv[0]` is an existing directory, so the final `else` reproduces the original command.
- Running a script (e.g. `manage.py`) or `django-admin`: `__main__.__spec__ is None` → falls through, unchanged.

The `-W<warnoption>` prefix and the Windows `.exe` / `-script.py` fallbacks are preserved untouched. `import django.__main__` is no longer needed inside this function and should be removed (keep the `import __main__` local).

## Tests to update

`tests/utils_tests/test_autoreload.py` relies on `sys.argv[0]` / `django.__main__.__file__` to exercise the module path, so these need to reflect the `__spec__` mechanism.

- `TestChildArguments.test_run_as_module` (line 159): currently mocks only `sys.argv = [django.__main__.__file__, 'runserver']` and expects `[python, '-m', 'django', 'runserver']`. It must additionally patch `__main__.__spec__` to a spec whose `parent == 'django'` (e.g. `django.__main__.__spec__` via `importlib.import_module('django.__main__').__spec__`, or `mock.Mock(parent='django')`). Without this it now returns the non-`-m` form, because during the test run `__main__` is `runtests.py` (`__spec__ is None`).
- Add a case for a package other than Django: patch `__main__.__spec__` to `mock.Mock(parent='pkg_other_than_django')` and assert `[sys.executable, '-m', 'pkg_other_than_django', 'runserver']` (this is the scenario from the ticket).
- `test_warnoptions`, `test_exe_fallback`, `test_entrypoint_fallback`, `test_raises_runtimeerror`: these leave `__main__.__spec__` as `None` and should keep passing unchanged.
- `RestartWithReloaderTests.test_python_m_django` (line 445): currently mocks `django.__main__.__file__`; change it to patch `__main__.__spec__` (parent `'django'`) so the end-to-end `restart_with_reloader` expectation `[executable, '-Wall', '-m', 'django', 'runserver']` still holds.

## Verification

Use the provided environment:

```bash
/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python tests/runtests.py \
    utils_tests.test_autoreload.TestChildArguments \
    utils_tests.test_autoreload.RestartWithReloaderTests -v2
```

I manually confirmed in this environment (`Python 3.6.13`) that `python -m pkg` yields `__main__.__spec__.parent == 'pkg'`, `python -m django` yields `'django'`, `python <dir>` yields `''`, and running a plain script yields `__main__.__spec__ is None`, so the branch conditions above behave as described.

## Scope

One source file (`django/utils/autoreload.py`) plus its test module. No public API, settings, or docs changes are required. Python 3.6 (the repo's minimum) supports `__main__.__spec__`.

# Plan

## Problem

`models.W042` is emitted for child models that inherit their primary key from a concrete parent model. The check in `Model._check_default_pk` (`django/db/models/base.py:1298`) flags any model whose `_meta.pk.auto_created` is true:

```python
if (
    cls._meta.pk.auto_created and
    not settings.is_overridden('DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD') and
    not cls._meta.app_config._is_default_auto_field_overridden
):
```

When a child inherits a table from a concrete parent, Django promotes the auto-created parent link (`OneToOneField`, `parent_link=True`) to be the child's primary key. That field has `auto_created=True`, so the check fires even though the developer did not leave the PK undefined.

I confirmed this directly against the frozen repository. With a `Parent` declaring `id = BigAutoField(primary_key=True)` and a `Child(Parent)`:

- `Child._meta.pk` is `check_framework.Child.parent_ptr`, a `OneToOneField` with `auto_created=True`, `is_relation=True`, `remote_field.parent_link=True`.
- `Child._check_default_pk()` currently returns a `W042` warning.
- A `Plain` model with a genuinely auto-created `id = AutoField` returns the same warning and should continue to.
- `Parent._meta.pk.auto_created` is `False`, so the parent is correctly not flagged.

The auto-created parent-link PK is the only case where an auto-created PK is a relation, so the fix is to skip relation PKs.

## Proposed change

In `django/db/models/base.py`, `Model._check_default_pk`, add a `not cls._meta.pk.is_relation` guard:

```python
if (
    cls._meta.pk.auto_created and
    not cls._meta.pk.is_relation and
    not settings.is_overridden('DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD') and
    not cls._meta.app_config._is_default_auto_field_overridden
):
```

This leaves the warning intact for ordinary auto-created `AutoField`/`BigAutoField` PKs (which are not relations) while suppressing it for inherited parent-link PKs. No import changes are needed; `is_relation` is available on every field.

I verified the corrected predicate against the reproduction above: `Child` goes from emitting `W042` to emitting nothing, while `Plain` still emits `W042`.

## Test to add

In `tests/check_framework/test_model_checks.py`, within `ModelDefaultAutoFieldTests` (which already patches `is_overridden` and sets `DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD='django.db.models.AutoField'`), add a regression test asserting no warning for an inherited manually specified PK:

```python
def test_inherited_auto_created_pk(self):
    class Parent(models.Model):
        id = models.BigAutoField(primary_key=True)

    class Child(Parent):
        pass

    self.assertEqual(checks.run_checks(app_configs=self.apps.get_app_configs()), [])
```

The existing `test_auto_created_pk` continues to cover the true-positive case (a model with no PK). The two tests together confirm the guard does not over-suppress.

## Notes / uncertainty

The issue text also mentions abstract parents, but an abstract parent's PK is copied to the child as a concrete, non-relation field (`auto_created=False`), so it is already not flagged; no separate handling is required. The only behavioral change is for concrete inheritance, which is exactly the reported bug.

# Plan

## Problem

`ModelChoiceField` (and thus subclasses and `ModelMultipleChoiceField`, which share the same message via inheritance) raises its `invalid_choice` error without telling the user *which* value was rejected. The sibling fields in `django/forms/fields.py` already do this:

- `ChoiceField.default_error_messages['invalid_choice']` = `'Select a valid choice. %(value)s is not one of the available choices.'` and its `validate()` passes `params={'value': value}`.
- `ModelMultipleChoiceField` already uses the same `%(value)s` form.

Only `ModelChoiceField` keeps the old, value-less wording, and its `to_python()` raises without `params`. The fix is to align `ModelChoiceField` with `ChoiceField`.

## Change 1 — `django/forms/models.py`

In `ModelChoiceField`:

1. Update the default message (around line 1191):

```python
default_error_messages = {
    'invalid_choice': _('Select a valid choice. %(value)s is not one of the'
                        ' available choices.'),
}
```

2. Pass the offending value in `to_python()` (around line 1287), matching the `ChoiceField.validate()` pattern:

```python
raise ValidationError(
    self.error_messages['invalid_choice'],
    code='invalid_choice',
    params={'value': value},
)
```

`ModelMultipleChoiceField` inherits `ModelChoiceField`'s `default_error_messages` dict via normal class-attribute lookup only where not overridden — it *does* override `invalid_choice` with the identical `%(value)s` string, so no change is needed there. Its `_check_values()` already passes `params={'value': val}`.

Note the value passed for a wrong-model instance is converted earlier in `to_python` (`value = getattr(value, key)` when `isinstance(value, self.queryset.model)`), but for a wrong model type that line is skipped, so `value` is the model instance itself and `%(value)s` renders its `str()`. This matches how `ChoiceField` interpolates arbitrary inputs, so no special-casing is required.

## Change 2 — Update tests that assert the old wording

The string `"Select a valid choice. That choice is not one of the available choices."` appears in the test suite and must be updated to include the interpolated value. Exact replacement text depends on the value in each test; the affected sites are:

- `tests/model_forms/test_modelchoicefield.py:54` — deleted Category's `c4.id` value.
- `tests/model_forms/test_modelchoicefield.py:62` — a `Book` instance passed to a `Category` field; renders as the book's `str()`.
- `tests/model_forms/test_modelchoicefield.py:219` — `test_disabled_modelchoicefield`: the field is disabled, so `bound_data` returns the initial value; the failing value is the initial author's prepared pk.
- `tests/model_forms/tests.py:1678` — `'writer'` error on an invalid FK; value is `w.pk` (an int).
- `tests/model_formsets/tests.py:1751` and `:1766` — error under `'id'`; values are the submitted ids.
- `tests/admin_widgets/tests.py:246` (`test_nonexistent_target_id`, deleted band pk) and `:254` (`test_invalid_target_id`, one of `'Iñtërnâtiônàlizætiøn'`, `"1234'"`, `-1234`).

For the admin tests, `assertContains` checks the rendered page, so the asserted substring must include the interpolated value (e.g. the nonexistent pk for the first test, and each `test_str` for the loop in the second). The two tests may need to loop over expected values.

The right way to pin these down is to run the suite after Change 1 and read the actual messages, rather than guessing the exact `str()` output (e.g. `Book`'s `__str__`, or how a deleted pk renders). Verify with:

```

    model_formsets.tests admin_widgets.tests forms_tests.tests.test_error_messages
```

`tests/forms_tests/tests/test_error_messages.py` also has a `ModelChoiceFieldErrorMessagesTestCase` that supplies a custom `invalid_choice` message ('INVALID CHOICE') — because a fully custom message lacks `%(value)s`, `ValidationError` will not attempt interpolation for that key in Django's message rendering, so that test should continue to pass unchanged. Confirm this while running the file.

Given a model with a foreign key relation to another model that has a non-auto CharField as its primary key:

	order.save()
	assert Order.objects.filter(product=order.product).exists() # succeeds

# Plan

## Problem

When a related object is assigned to a foreign key before its primary key (or `to_field`) value is set, and that value is assigned afterwards, saving the child stores an empty local FK value instead of the related object's key. The offending logic is in `Model._prepare_related_fields_for_save()` at `django/db/models/base.py:911`.

## Root cause

At assignment time, `ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.__set__` copies the related object's target value into the local FK column:

```python
# django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py
for lh_field, rh_field in self.field.related_fields:
    setattr(instance, lh_field.attname, getattr(value, rh_field.attname))
```

For an auto integer PK, the value is `None` at that moment. For a `CharField` PK (or a `to_field` pointing at a non-PK `CharField`), `getattr(value, rh_field.attname)` returns `''`, because `Field._get_default` returns `str` for empty-string-allowed fields (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:861`).

Later, when the parent is populated and saved, `_prepare_related_fields_for_save` only refreshes the child's local FK value when it is explicitly `None`:

```python
# django/db/models/base.py:936 (base commit)
elif getattr(self, field.attname) is None:
    # Use pk from related object if it has been saved after
    # an assignment.
    setattr(self, field.attname, obj.pk)
```

Since the stored value is `''`, this branch never runs, `''` is written to the FK column, and the reference is lost. (The same check also uses `obj.pk`, which is wrong for a `ForeignKey(..., to_field=...)` whose target is not the PK.)

## Proposed change

In `django/db/models/base.py`, treat any *empty* FK value (not just `None`) as "not yet set", and refill it from the related object's **target field** value rather than `obj.pk`:

```python
elif getattr(self, field.attname) in field.empty_values:
    # Use the target field value from the related object if it
    # has been set after an assignment.
    setattr(self, field.attname, getattr(obj, field.target_field.attname))
```

Why this exact form:

- `field.empty_values` is inherited from `Field` (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:91`, `[None, '', [], (), {}]`). `ForeignKey` does not override it, so `''` is included. This is the same attribute the insert path already uses to treat empty values (`base.py:1255`).
- `field.target_field.attname` is the column the FK actually stores, and the very next line (`base.py:942`) already compares against it. Using it (instead of `obj.pk`) makes the branch correct for both a non-auto PK and a `to_field` that is not the PK.
- The preceding `if obj.pk is None:` guard is unchanged, so an unsaved related object still raises the "prohibited to prevent data loss" `ValueError`.

## Regression test

Add a test covering the issue. `tests/many_to_one/models.py` currently has no model with a non-auto primary key, so add one (the file is a test app without migrations, so no migration is needed):

```python
class NonAutoPk(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(primary_key=True, max_length=20)
```

and a corresponding `tests/many_to_one/tests.py` test (mirrors the report):

```python
def test_save_after_related_object_pk_set(self):
    parent = NonAutoPk()
    child = Child(parent=parent)          # or a FK to NonAutoPk
    parent.name = 'foo'
    parent.save()
    child.save()
    self.assertEqual(Child.objects.get(pk=child.pk).parent_id, 'foo')
```

(If a dedicated FK model is preferred, add `parent = models.ForeignKey(NonAutoPk, models.CASCADE)` alongside `NonAutoPk`.) The existing `ToFieldChild`/`Parent` pair can additionally be used to lock in the `to_field` behavior:

```python
def test_save_after_related_object_to_field_set(self):
    parent = Parent()
    child = ToFieldChild(parent=parent)
    parent.name = 'jeff'
    parent.save()
    child.save()
    self.assertEqual(ToFieldChild.objects.get(pk=child.pk).parent_id, 'jeff')
```

## Verification performed

- Reproduced on the frozen base commit with a minimal standalone script: after `order.product = Product(); order.product.sku = "foo"; order.product.save(); order.save()`, `product_id` remained `''` and `Order.objects.filter(product_id="").exists()` returned `True`.
- Applied the proposed change: `product_id` becomes `'foo'`, the empty-string row no longer exists, and `Order.objects.filter(product=order.product)` resolves. The `to_field='name'` variant (which raised `IntegrityError` with the `obj.pk`-based variant) also resolves to `'jeff'`.
- Ran the existing suites `many_to_one`, `one_to_one`, `model_fields`, `bulk_create`, `model_inheritance`, and `select_related` — all pass with the change. (`foreign_keys` fails identically on the unmodified tree because that test module does not exist, so it is not a regression.)

# Plan

## Problem

On `INSERT`, values returned by the database for `returning_fields` (e.g. an auto-generated primary key) are copied straight onto the model instance without running any database converters. Query paths (`SELECT`) do run them, so a field that overrides `from_db_value` (or relies on backend converters) yields a wrapper instance when loaded, but a raw DB value after `create()`/`save()`/`bulk_create()`.

Evidence:
- `django/db/models/base.py:871-874` — `Model._save_table` takes `results[0]` from `_do_insert` and does `setattr(self, field.attname, value)` with no conversion.
- `django/db/models/query.py:506-521` — `bulk_create` also does `setattr(obj, field.attname, result)` directly.
- `django/db/models/sql/compiler.py:1403-1421` — `SQLInsertCompiler.execute_sql` fetches returned rows (`fetch_returned_insert_rows` / `fetch_returned_insert_columns` / `last_insert_id`) and returns them raw.
- The conversion machinery already exists and is used by `SELECT`: `SQLCompiler.get_converters` / `apply_converters` (`django/db/models/sql/compiler.py:1100-1122`), driven by `Field.get_db_converters` (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:746`, includes `from_db_value`) plus `connection.ops.get_db_converters` (`django/db/backends/base/operations.py:577`).

Key detail: `SQLCompiler.get_converters` expects expression objects, not bare fields. Backend `get_db_converters` implementations read `expression.output_field.get_internal_type()`, and `Col.get_db_converters` (`django/db/models/expressions.py:847`) delegates to `target`/`output_field`. A raw `Field` has no `output_field`, so the returning fields must be wrapped as `Col` expressions via `field.get_col(...)` — the same representation the `SELECT` path uses.

## Change

### 1. `django/db/models/sql/compiler.py` — `SQLInsertCompiler.execute_sql`

Rewrite `execute_sql` so it (a) builds a `Col` expression for each returned column, (b) computes converters with the inherited `self.get_converters(...)`, and (c) applies them via `self.apply_converters(...)` before returning. `SQLInsertCompiler` already inherits both methods from `SQLCompiler`, so no new helper is needed.

    def execute_sql(self, returning_fields=None):
        assert not (
            returning_fields and len(self.query.objs) != 1 and
            not self.connection.features.can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert
        )
        opts = self.query.get_meta()
        self.returning_fields = returning_fields
        cols = []
        with self.connection.cursor() as cursor:
            for sql, params in self.as_sql():
                cursor.execute(sql, params)
            if not self.returning_fields:
                return []
            if self.connection.features.can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert and len(self.query.objs) > 1:
                rows = self.connection.ops.fetch_returned_insert_rows(cursor)
                cols = [field.get_col(opts.db_table) for field in self.returning_fields]
            elif self.connection.features.can_return_columns_from_insert:
                assert len(self.query.objs) == 1
                rows = [self.connection.ops.fetch_returned_insert_columns(cursor, self.returning_params)]
                cols = [field.get_col(opts.db_table) for field in self.returning_fields]
            else:
                # Backends without RETURNING return only the pk via last_insert_id.
                rows = [(
                    self.connection.ops.last_insert_id(
                        cursor, opts.db_table, opts.pk.column
                    ),
                )]
                cols = [opts.pk.get_col(opts.db_table)]
        converters = self.get_converters(cols)
        if converters:
            rows = list(self.apply_converters(rows, converters))
        return rows

Notes on why this shape is required:
- `get_converters`/`apply_converters` iterate the row positions, so `cols` must line up 1:1 with the returned columns for each branch. The two RETURNING branches return `len(returning_fields)` columns; the `last_insert_id` branch returns exactly the pk column.
- `apply_converters` is a generator yielding lists, but callers index/zip the result (`base.py:874` uses `results[0]`; `_batched_insert` `extend`s), so it must be materialized with `list(...)`.
- The converter functions are field/backend agnostic (`value, expression, connection`), so both `from_db_value` overrides and built-in backend coercions (e.g. SQLite datetime/decimal) now run for inserted values.
- Converters are applied only to freshly fetched rows, so there is no double conversion and no behavior change for fields without converters.

No changes are needed in `base.py`, `query.py`, or `options.py`: they already consume the rows returned by `execute_sql`, and this fix routes inserted values through the identical machinery the `SELECT` path uses.

### 2. Tests

Add a model to `tests/queries/models.py` with a `db_returning` field that overrides `from_db_value`, mirroring the issue. A pk `AutoField` subclass is the simplest reproduction because `AutoFieldMixin.db_returning = True` (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:2451`), so it is always a returning field:

    class CustomAutoField(models.BigAutoField):
        def from_db_value(self, value, expression, connection):
            if value is None:
                return None
            return CustomWrapper(value)   # small local wrapper class

        def get_prep_value(self, value):
            if value is None:
                return None
            return value.value if isinstance(value, CustomWrapper) else value


    class CustomAutoFieldModel(models.Model):
        id = CustomAutoField(primary_key=True)

Add tests in `tests/queries/test_db_returning.py` asserting the converted instance is produced after insert:
- `create()` returns a converted value on the pk (covers the `last_insert_id` branch on SQLite and the `can_return_columns_from_insert` branch on PostgreSQL/Oracle/MySQL).
- `bulk_create()` sets converted values on every object, gated with `@skipUnlessDBFeature('can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert')`.
- Optionally `save()` on an existing pk-less instance.

Because the un-gated single-row test exercises the `last_insert_id` branch, it runs against the default SQLite test backend; the bulk test needs a backend with `can_return_rows_from_bulk_insert` (PostgreSQL).

## Verification

- Run the targeted suites against the default backend: `cd /testbed/tests && /opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python runtests.py from_db_value queries.test_db_returning bulk_create -v 1`.
- The new un-gated insert test should fail before the fix (raw int) and pass after; the bulk test is skipped on SQLite but should pass on PostgreSQL.
- Existing `test_db_returning.py` assertions (`RETURNING ...` SQL text, `datetime` conversion on `NonIntegerPKReturningModel.created`) must still pass, confirming converters do not disturb SQL generation or already-correct values.

# Plan

## Problem

`Q(...) & Exists(...)` raises `TypeError`, while `Exists(...) & Q(...)` works.

`Q.__and__` delegates to `Q._combine`, whose first line is a strict type check:

```python
# django/db/models/query_utils.py, Q._combine
if not isinstance(other, Q):
    raise TypeError(other)
```

Since `Exists` is not a `Q` subclass, the left-hand operand `Q()` rejects it. The reverse order works because `Exists` inherits from `Expression` → `Combinable`, and `Combinable.__and__` (django/db/models/expressions.py) is written to accept any `conditional` operand and builds `Q(self) & Q(other)`.

Python calls the left operand's `__and__` first and only falls back to `__rand__` if that returns `NotImplemented`. `Q.__and__` is defined and raises instead, so `__rand__` on `Exists`/`Combinable` is never reached — the missing piece is not a `__rand__`, it is the too-narrow check in `Q._combine`.

## Evidence

- `django/db/models/query_utils.py`: `Q._combine` rejects anything that is not `isinstance(other, Q)`; `Q.conditional = True` is already declared on the class.
- `django/db/models/expressions.py`: `Combinable.__and__` / `__or__` gate on `getattr(self, 'conditional', False) and getattr(other, 'conditional', False)`, and `Exists` reports `conditional == True` (its `output_field` is `BooleanField`). This is the exact condition on which boolean `&`/`|` is considered valid elsewhere in the ORM.
- Confirmed on the frozen checkout: `Exists(...) & Q()` returns a plain `Q`; `Q() & Exists(...)` raises `TypeError` at `Query_utils.py` line 73.
- Existing regression guard `tests/queries/test_q.py::QTests.test_combine_not_q_object` expects `Q(x=1) & object()` to still raise `TypeError(str(obj))`, so the fix must continue to reject non-conditional operands.

## Proposed change

In `django/db/models/query_utils.py`, replace the strict type check with the same `conditional` predicate the rest of the ORM uses:

```python
def _combine(self, other, conn):
    if getattr(other, 'conditional', False) is False:
        raise TypeError(other)
    ...
```

The remaining body is unchanged: the `if not other:` branch only triggers for a falsy operand (an empty `Q`), while a truthy conditional expression such as `Exists` falls through to `obj.add(...)`, producing `<Q: (AND: ('x', 1), <Exists>)>`. An empty `Q()` combined with `Exists` returns a copy of `Exists`, mirroring the `Exists & Q()` behaviour.

I verified this one-line change against the provided environment:
- `Q() & Exists(...)`, `Q(x=1) & Exists(...)`, and `Q() | Exists(...)` all succeed and produce combined `Q` objects.
- `Q() & object()` still raises `TypeError`.
- `Q() & Q()`, `Q(x=1) & Q()`, and the empty-`Q` short-circuit tests continue to pass.

## Tests

Run `tests/queries/test_q.py` (covers empty/non-`Q` operands) and the boolean-combination test in `tests/expressions/tests.py` (`BasicExpressionsTests.test_boolean_expression_combined`, currently only exercising `Exists & Q`).

Add a regression case for the reversed order the issue reports. The natural home is `BasicExpressionsTests.test_boolean_expression_combined` in `tests/expressions/tests.py`, which already has `is_ceo`/`is_poc` querysets and an `Employee`/`Company` fixture:

```python
self.assertCountEqual(
    Employee.objects.filter(Q(salary__gte=30) & Exists(is_ceo)),
    [self.max],
)
```

Optionally also assert the non-database form in `tests/queries/test_q.py` to lock in that an empty `Q()` combined with a conditional expression returns that expression when it is the reverse operand, mirroring the existing `test_combine_and_empty` / `test_combine_or_empty` patterns.

## Out of scope

`Exists & Q()` retains `dict`/`tuple`-style payloads through the existing `if not other` branch; making the two operand orders produce byte-identical trees is not required to fix the reported `TypeError` and would change established behaviour. The `Combinable.__rand__` / `__ror__` methods remain as-is (they are only reached for non-`Q` left operands).

# Plan

## Problem and root cause

`MultiValueField.clean()` in `django/forms/fields.py` (currently around lines 1015–1058) has an early return that fires *before* the per-subfield loop:

```python
def clean(self, value):
    clean_data = []
    errors = []
    ...
    if not value or isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
        if not value or not [v for v in value if v not in self.empty_values]:
            if self.required:
                raise ValidationError(self.error_messages['required'], code='required')
            else:
                return self.compress([])          # <-- unconditional short-circuit
    else:
        raise ValidationError(self.error_messages['invalid'], code='invalid')
    for i, field in enumerate(self.fields):
        ...
        if field_value in self.empty_values:
            if self.require_all_fields:
                if self.required:
                    raise ValidationError(self.error_messages['required'], code='required')
            elif field.required:
                # add 'incomplete' error and skip cleaning
                ...
```

Whenever *all* submitted values are empty and the `MultiValueField` itself is `required=False`, execution returns `self.compress([])` immediately. It never reaches the `elif field.required:` branch that emits the `incomplete` error for a required subfield. So a field built with `require_all_fields=False`, `required=False`, and a mix of required/optional subfields treats "all empty" as valid.

The per-subfield branch already behaves correctly for the "partially filled" case, which is why the issue's second example (`mf_0='xxx', mf_1=''`) already returns invalid.

I reproduced the issue on the frozen commit:

```
all empty valid -> True
second empty valid -> False <ul class="errorlist">... Enter a complete value.
```

## Proposed change

Guard the short-circuit so it only applies when the field is *also* free of required subfields:

```python
                if self.required:
                    raise ValidationError(self.error_messages['required'], code='required')
                elif not any(field.required for field in self.fields):
                    return self.compress([])
```

This is the minimal change: it only turns the early return into a conditional, and lets the existing loop handle the required-subfield case (adding `incomplete` errors and raising `ValidationError(errors)` before `compress()` is reached).

Resulting behavior:

| `required` | `require_all_fields` | subfields | all-empty result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `True` | either | any | `required` error (unchanged) |
| `False` | `True` | all forced optional in `__init__` | `compress([])` (unchanged) |
| `False` | `False` | all optional | `compress([])` (`not any(...)` is True) |
| `False` | `False` | at least one required | falls through to loop, raises `incomplete` (the fix) |

Cases that must stay unchanged and why:
- `require_all_fields=True` (`__init__` sets every subfield `required = False`) keeps the `not any(field.required ...)` guard true and still returns `compress([])`.
- `SplitDateTimeField` (`SplitDateTimeField` uses the `require_all_fields=True` default) is unaffected.
- `BaseRangeField` in `django/contrib/postgres/forms/ranges.py` passes `required=False` and `require_all_fields=False` but constructs both subfields with `required=False`, so `not any(field.required ...)` is still true and it keeps returning `None`.

I confirmed the change works by temporarily applying it and driving the affected fields directly. With the guard in place, the reported field validates all-empty input as invalid, while `PhoneField(required=False)` (require_all_fields defaulting to `True`) still returns `None`. The working tree has already been restored to the original file.

## Test updates

**Existing test that changes behavior** — `tests/forms_tests/tests/test_forms.py::test_multivalue_optional_subfields` (around lines 3091–3095):

```python
        # For an optional `MultiValueField` with `require_all_fields=False`, we
        # don't get any `required` error but we still get `incomplete` errors.
        f = PhoneField(required=False, require_all_fields=False)
        self.assertIsNone(f.clean(''))
        self.assertIsNone(f.clean(None))
        self.assertIsNone(f.clean([]))
```

Under the fix these three calls raise `incomplete` instead of returning `None` (the field has required subfields), so they must be converted to `assertRaisesMessage(ValidationError, "'Enter a complete value.', 'Enter an extension.'")` (or an equivalent assertion on the collected messages). The subsequent `f.clean(['+61'])` case is unchanged.

**New regression coverage.** Add a case built from the issue to `test_multivalue_field_validation` (or a focused new test) that constructs a `MultiValueField` with `CharField(required=False)` and `CharField(required=True)`, `require_all_fields=False`, `required=False`, and asserts:
- `clean(['', ''])` raises `incomplete` (was previously accepted);
- `clean(['xxx', ''])` raises `incomplete` (already worked);
- fully populated input still succeeds.

## Verification

Run the focused form tests, then the broader forms suite and the PostgreSQL range form tests (which also use `require_all_fields=False`):

```
/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python tests/runtests.py \
    forms_tests.tests.test_forms.FormsTestCase.test_multivalue_optional_subfields \
    forms_tests.tests.test_forms.FormsTestCase.test_multivalue_field_validation -v2

/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python tests/runtests.py forms_tests -v0
/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python tests/runtests.py postgres_tests.test_ranges -v0
```

## Notes / scope

- The `require_all_fields` documentation in `docs/ref/forms/fields.txt` already states that an `incomplete` error is raised when a required subfield is empty, so no doc change is strictly needed; a sentence clarifying that this also applies when *all* values are empty is optional.
- The fix is confined to `django/forms/fields.py`; no other production module needs touching. The main risk is the intentional behavior change for all-empty input on optional `MultiValueField`s that declare required subfields, which is exactly what the issue asks for and is covered by the updated test.

Copying '/home/vagrant/python/lib/python2.7/site-packages/django/contrib/admin/static/admin/css/base.css'
Post-processed 'admin/css/base.css' as 'admin/css/base.6b517d0d5813.css'
